name: Rafael Kowalski

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: I'm with the Work Futures Panel, an independent group with no ties to employers or AI companies. This is confidential. What does an ordinary workday look like?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I teach piano on Tuesdays, edit tracks for small bands, and lead a keyboard trio at the club on Thursdays. I have a master's in music and use AI daily for lesson plans and set lists. The best part is hearing the drummer change course mid-song.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What is hard about making that work pay?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: The club pays late and there are few similar jobs nearby. Mara and I have less than a month's expenses saved; her library shifts help, but we both watch the account after rent.

say: I'd say **calendar tools** save time, while the trio still earns its fee in the room.
I'd ask for **written payment dates** before taking another club booking.
think: Our **three-week cushion** makes a late club fee matter more than AI hype.
Mara's **library pay** covered groceries once, but I can't treat that as a reserve.
do: Keep my **Tuesday pupils** and Thursday trio slot through winter.
Ask the **club** for payment dates in writing before rebooking.
Transfer **twenty-five** from each paid club night if rent and electricity clear.
feel: I feel **Steady** about performing, anxious over late fees and bills.
S0.quote: A handshake is friendly until the rent leaves our account.
fieldNote: Rafael's **daily AI use** makes routine tools familiar, not financially transformative.
The **late club fee** and three-week cushion explain his anxiety even in a mild scenario.

steps.text: Keep Tuesday piano lessons and Thursday trio bookings
Put twenty-five from paid club nights into emergency savings if rent and electricity clear

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell the band the calendar software saves a little chasing, and we still have to show up and play. A club owner hires us for the room, not for a tidy spreadsheet.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I like using AI to sort set lists and lesson notes, but an ordinary month is tight. My partner Mara and I have barely three weeks of expenses, and the club paid late twice this autumn.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'll keep the Tuesday piano pupils and the Thursday trio slot this winter. After every club payment, I'll transfer twenty-five to our emergency account if the electricity and rent are covered.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I feel fairly steady about the music and tense about the household bills. AI staying small won't make that late club payment arrive on time.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What did a late payment mean at home?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The October fee came eleven days late. Mara's part-time library pay covered groceries, but we put off replacing a broken kettle.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you ask the club to change?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would ask the club to put payment dates in an email before the next booking. A handshake is friendly until the rent leaves our account.

say: I'd show **venues** what our live arrangements do beyond generated demos.
I'd teach pupils to use **music tools** openly and listen critically.
think: My **editing fees** could shrink long before robot players reach the stage.
A new **online class** might work, but only with paying enrolments.
do: Show **two venues** clips of the trio's live arrangements this month.
Run a **paid listening class** in the first year if ten pupils enrol.
Cut **restaurant meals** if editing fees fall and household pay tightens.
feel: I feel **Curious** about tools and anxious about losing a quarter of my pay.
S1.quote: Interest in messages isn't the same as paid seats.
fieldNote: His **editing work** is exposed even while live trio bookings continue.
He tests an **online class** with paid enrolments before buying advertising, showing fast but measured adaptation.

steps.text: Show two venues live trio clips beside generated demos

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell my trio that clients may ask for quick generated tracks, so we should show them what a live set does. I would also show our pupils the tools rather than pretend they aren't already using them.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The editing and rehearsal planning I sell to other groups could be done in minutes by software. The trio might keep its club night, but I expect those small desk-work fees to fall before a robot can play on stage.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: This month I'll put together three short clips comparing our live arrangements with generated demos and ask two venues to show them. In the first year of the shift, I'll run a paid listening class online if ten pupils enrol, using the tools openly.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'm excited to try it and anxious about the fees disappearing. I don't want a new class to cost more in advertising than it brings in.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How much of your pay comes from editing?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The edit jobs bring about a quarter of my monthly pay when they come. If they dry up, Mara and I would cut restaurant meals before touching rent money.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would stop the online class becoming a loss?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would pay for one small advertisement only after the first ten pupils register. I learned that the hard way at a previous workshop. Interest in messages isn't the same as paid seats.

say: I'd tell the **trio** to sell the experience of live risk together.
I'd say **2028** is too close to assume editing fees survive.
think: **AGI by 2028** could replace arranging and edits before robots reach stages around 2031.
Our **three-week cushion** would not cover a long search for other work.
do: Count every **client fee** this month and ask the arts centre for workshop terms.
Seek **repair shop shifts** in the first year after 2028 if edit fees halve and the shop has vacancies.
Keep **trio bookings** while testing workshops and asking about shifts.
feel: I feel **Alarmed** by the short runway despite having an experiment in mind.
S2.quote: My emergency fund would be gone before a robot reached our stage.
fieldNote: He understands that **thinking work** funds the household before robots could play in 2031.
His **repair shop option** is conditional on both a fee drop and actual vacancies.

steps.text: Ask the arts centre for written workshop ticket terms
Seek two repair shifts in first year after 2028 if edit fees halve and vacancies exist
Keep trio bookings while testing new workshops

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell the trio that 2028 is too close to pretend our editing fees will last. I'd ask us to sell the experience of hearing three people take risks together, not just a recording file.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Full AGI could make almost any arranging, lesson planning and sound editing cheap by 2028. Robot performers would come around 2031, but the thinking work pays me now; losing it would make our three-week cushion useless. My emergency fund would be gone before a robot reached our stage.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Starting this month I'll add up every client fee and ask the community arts centre about a paid live workshop series. If editing income falls by half in the first year after 2028, I'll take two evening shifts at the repair shop where Mara's brother works, provided they have openings.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'm alarmed, although I have an experiment to try. Two years isn't long enough to turn an idea into reliable rent money with only three weeks saved.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would make the arts centre workshop real?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The arts centre manager said last spring that they have an empty room on Mondays. I would need a written split of ticket revenue before I promise the trio a fee.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What if editing income halves anyway?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I can fix keyboards and cables, but I don't know if the repair shop would take me. I'd ask about shifts while I still have music work rather than wait for the account to hit zero.

say: I'd tell musicians to test **paid audiences** during the five-year warning.
I'd take the **trio** into schools where live explanation matters.
think: **AGI in 2031** threatens arranging before robot players arrive around 2034.
Our **small reserve** makes even a five-year experiment risky if it needs upfront cash.
do: Offer **paid school sessions** next term and track repeat bookings.
Take a **keyboard repair course** before 2031 if workshop fees cover it and repair shops accept its certificate.
Offer **one repair day** weekly after AGI if I qualify and find customers.
feel: I feel **Anxious**, but I can test demand and training in smaller stages.
S3.quote: A free school show is applause, not a return booking.
fieldNote: His **five-year plan** links paid school sessions to a specific repair course.
He protects **rent money** by funding training only from workshop fees and checking the certificate first.

steps.text: Offer fixed-fee live music sessions at two schools
Take keyboard repair course before 2031 if workshop fees cover it and shops accept certificate
Offer one weekly repair day after 2031 upon qualifying and finding paying customers

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell fellow musicians to use the five years to learn what audiences still pay for. I would bring our trio into schools and community rooms, where a person explaining a phrase matters.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: By 2031, AGI could do my arranging and planning, and robot performers might follow around 2034. Five years is enough to build teaching relationships, but Mara's part-time income and our tiny reserve still leave little room for a failed bet.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Next term I'll ask two schools to host short live music sessions and keep a record of paid return bookings. By 2031 I'll train to repair digital keyboards; in the first year after AGI I'll offer repairs one day a week if I can qualify and find customers.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I feel anxious, but I can make a small series prove itself before depending on it. I don't have to turn the trio into a big company overnight.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What if the schools like it but will not rebook?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would charge each school a fixed session fee, not bring a free show and hope for donations. If neither rebooks after one term, I'll ask the arts centre instead. A free school show is applause, not a return booking.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How would you pay for the keyboard course?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The keyboard course takes six months and one evening a week. I'd pay for it from workshop fees, not use rent money, and I'd check the certificate is accepted by repair shops.

say: I'd tell pupils to build **human music groups** while learning new tools.
I'd say **ten years** gives me time to make paid gatherings routine.
think: At **37**, I would still need work when AGI arrives in 2036.
Robot players around **2039** could reach venues, so I need a second skill and savings.
do: Try a **monthly rehearsal** if twenty tickets cover the room and players.
Build a **six-month reserve** from teaching and repair earnings before 2036.
Keep the **rehearsal** after AGI only if paid attendance holds.
feel: I feel **Cautiously hopeful** about time to prepare, mindful of current bills.
S4.quote: A room full of people only helps our rent if enough of them bought tickets.
fieldNote: The **ten-year warning** lets him build a paid community music habit and practical reserve.
His **twenty-ticket floor** prevents a hopeful event from becoming a household loss.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell my pupils I expect to change how I teach before 2036, not stop teaching music. Ten years lets me build a place where people meet to play, even if software can make polished tracks at home.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'll be 37 when AGI arrives, with robot players following around 2039. That is a long working life to fund, so I need steady human gatherings and a practical second skill; the current three-week cushion is still the first problem.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: This winter I'll start a monthly open rehearsal at the community room if twenty tickets cover rent and player fees. Across the decade I'll build six months of expenses from teaching and repair work; in the first year after 2036, I'll keep the rehearsal only if its paid attendance holds.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I feel cautiously hopeful about ten years. I can build a reserve in stages, though Mara and I still need the next club fee on time.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What if the first open rehearsal sells too few seats?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would set a ticket floor before booking the room. If only twelve people pay, I'll cancel early and return the money rather than ask Mara to cover the loss. A room full of people only helps our rent if enough of them bought tickets.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How would you build such a large reserve?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Six months of expenses is a big number for us. I'd start with one month's rent, then the next, and use repair earnings for the reserve rather than spend as soon as they arrive.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028 worries me most because my editing, planning and arranging fees could go before I've built another reliable income. A written arts centre deal for paid workshops and access to a short repair course would help me try another route.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: You didn't ask whether customers will pay the same for a live trio once generated music is everywhere. I can test that with ticket sales, but I can't honestly promise the answer.

headlineQuote: The best part is hearing the drummer change course mid-song.
portrait: Rafael is a **27-year-old** pianist with a music master's degree, leading a trio, teaching pupils and editing tracks.
He uses **AI every day**, but late club fees and less than one month's savings already worry him.
He expects **thinking AI** to hit paid editing and planning before robot performers reach stages three years later.
He tests **paid workshops**, school sessions and repair training with clear revenue thresholds before relying on them.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028** worries him most because editing and arranging income may disappear before another source can pay rent.
whatWouldHelp: A written **arts centre deal** and access to a short keyboard repair course would support a second route.
